title: MMA as a League
bigQuestion: How did mixed martial arts go from a no-rules spectacle to a sport licensed by governments?

story.title: The Stamp on the Bout Sheet
story.kicker: A government stamp turns a fight card into a licensed event.
paragraphs: Before a professional mixed martial arts event in the United States, a state official checks a stack of paper. Each fighter needs a license, a medical clearance and a signed bout agreement. The official stamps the sheet that lists who meets whom, in which weight class, for how many rounds.

That stamp belongs to an *athletic commission*, a government office that regulates combat sports. The same kind of office had licensed boxing and pro wrestling for decades. In the early 1990s, most commissions had no rules at all for a sport called mixed martial arts.

The new sport was not an ancient art rediscovered in a lost temple. It was a business built by promoters, cable television and athletes trained in wrestling, boxing, judo, Brazilian jiu-jitsu and Muay Thai. Its rules were written in the late 1990s and 2000s by commissions and companies.

This chapter follows that paper trail. It starts with older mixed contests in Greece, Brazil and Japan. Then it follows one American company, its critics and the commissions that turned a spectacle into a league.
story.think: Why might a government want to license a sport it once tried to stop?

lessons.title: Pankration at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient Greeks held pankration, a contest joining boxing and wrestling, at the Olympic Games from 648 BCE.
reading: Ancient Greek writers record that *pankration* entered the Olympic Games at Olympia in 648 BCE. The name means all strength or all power. It combined elements of Greek boxing and Greek wrestling in one event. Athletes trained for it in the gymnasium, a Greek building for exercise and education.

Pankration still had rules and officials. Ancient sources say biting and gouging the eyes were banned, and referees carried rods to punish fouls. Athletes competed without weight classes, so heavier men held an advantage. Winners were honored with an olive wreath, as in other Olympic events.

Modern MMA promoters sometimes point to pankration as an ancestor. Historians note a long gap between the two. The ancient games ended in late antiquity, and no living line of pankration teachers connects Olympia to modern cages. The Roman emperor Theodosius I is often linked to the end of the games near 393 CE.

words.d: an ancient Greek Olympic contest that combined boxing and wrestling
the sanctuary in southern Greece where the ancient Olympic Games were held
an action a rule forbids, which officials punish

look.title: An Ancient Description
look.text: Philostratus, writing in the third century CE, says pankration allowed almost everything except biting and gouging, and that the Spartans alone allowed even those.
look.prompt: What does this description show about whether pankration had rules?

check.q: When did pankration enter the ancient Olympic Games?
check.why: Greek writers date pankration's first Olympic contest to 648 BCE.

check.q: Which actions did ancient sources say pankration banned?
check.why: Ancient sources record bans on biting and gouging.

check.q: Why do historians question pankration as MMA's direct ancestor?
choices: No living line of teachers connects Olympia to modern MMA
check.why: The ancient games ended long ago, and no teaching line survived to the present.

lessons.title: Vale Tudo in Brazil
lessons.mainIdea: In twentieth-century Brazil, open-rule contests called vale tudo and the Gracie family's challenges shaped Brazilian jiu-jitsu.
reading: In 1914 the Japanese judo teacher Mitsuyo Maeda arrived in Brazil after years of touring the Americas and Europe. He settled in Belém, in northern Brazil. Carlos Gracie, a son of a local family, studied with him. Maeda had trained at the Kodokan in Tokyo under Kanō Jigorō's system.

Carlos and his brothers, including Hélio Gracie, opened a school in Rio de Janeiro in the 1920s. They developed what became *Brazilian jiu-jitsu*. The family publicized it through open challenges to fighters from other arts. Later generations of the family spread the art across Brazil and abroad.

Brazilians called contests with very few rules *vale tudo*, Portuguese for anything goes. These events appeared in circuses and on Brazilian television over the century. They were public shows before any government wrote a rule book for them. Promoters sold tickets to crowds who came to see styles tested against each other.

words.d: Portuguese for anything goes; Brazilian contests with very few rules
a grappling art developed by the Gracie family in Brazil from Maeda's judo
a public invitation to fight a person from another style

check.why: Vale tudo is Portuguese for anything goes.

check.why: The Gracies issued public challenges to fighters of other styles.

lessons.title: Mixed Bouts in Japan
lessons.mainIdea: Japan hosted a famous boxer-versus-wrestler bout in 1976 and built organized mixed promotions such as Shooto and Pancrase before the UFC.
reading: On June 26, 1976, boxing champion Muhammad Ali met Japanese professional wrestler Antonio Inoki in Tokyo. The two sides fought over rules until days before the bout. It ended in a draw after fifteen rounds and disappointed many viewers. The bout was shown on closed-circuit television in many countries.

Japanese professional wrestling had a strong following, and some performers wanted real contests. Satoru Sayama founded *Shooto* in the mid-1980s as an organized sport with its own rules and amateur ranks. It is one of the earliest organized mixed martial arts bodies.

*Pancrase* began in Tokyo in September 1993, two months before the first UFC. Its name borrowed from the Greek pankration. Japan thus had rule-based mixed events before the American league existed. Its founders were professional wrestlers who wanted real, unscripted results.

words.d: a Japanese organization for rule-based mixed contests, founded by Satoru Sayama in the 1980s
a Japanese mixed contest promotion that began in 1993
a company that organizes, advertises and sells fight events

lessons.title: UFC 1 in Denver
lessons.mainIdea: The first Ultimate Fighting Championship was held in Denver on November 12, 1993, as a pay-per-view tournament between styles.
reading: The *Ultimate Fighting Championship* held its first event at McNichols Sports Arena in Denver, Colorado, on November 12, 1993. It was sold on *pay-per-view*, meaning cable viewers paid to watch one event. Semaphore Entertainment Group produced it with Art Davie and Rorion Gracie.

The event was an eight-man tournament. Its promoters matched fighters from different styles, including boxing, karate, sumo and savate. It was held in an eight-sided fenced ring that the company called the Octagon. Its bouts ended only by a stoppage, a knockout, or a fighter's corner giving up.

Royce Gracie, Rorion's younger brother, won the tournament. The event advertised Brazilian jiu-jitsu to American audiences. It had few rules, no weight classes and no time limits for its bouts. Rorion had moved from Brazil to California and taught jiu-jitsu there.

words.d: an American mixed martial arts promotion that held its first event in 1993
a way of selling one television event to cable viewers who pay to watch it
the UFC's name for its eight-sided fenced ring

lessons.title: Critics and Cable
lessons.mainIdea: In the mid-1990s critics led by Senator John McCain pushed states and cable companies to reject no-holds-barred events.
reading: Early UFC events were sold with slogans claiming there were no rules. Senator John McCain of Arizona, a boxing fan, watched a tape and campaigned against the events. He famously compared them to human cockfighting and wrote to state governors urging bans.

Many states refused to allow the events, and several major cable companies dropped them from pay-per-view by the late 1990s. Without cable, the company lost most of its audience. Events moved to smaller venues in places that would permit them. Promoters kept the events alive with smaller home video and live audiences.

Under that pressure, the promotion added rules. It introduced weight classes, rounds, gloves and a longer list of *fouls*. Historians see this as the point where a spectacle began turning into a sport that a commission could license. The company also began seeking approval from state athletic commissions.

words.d: a phrase meaning a contest with no limits, used to advertise early events
an official rule that forbids something
actions a rule book forbids, which officials punish

lessons.title: The Unified Rules
lessons.mainIdea: New Jersey regulators wrote the Unified Rules of Mixed Martial Arts in 2000 and 2001, the same year Zuffa bought the UFC.
reading: In 2000 the New Jersey State Athletic Control Board met with promoters, referees and doctors to write rules for mixed martial arts. The board adopted the *Unified Rules of Mixed Martial Arts* in 2001. They set weight classes, round lengths, required gloves and a list of fouls.

In January 2001 a company called *Zuffa*, owned by casino executives Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta with Dana White as president, bought the UFC. Zuffa worked to win approval from state commissions. Nevada, home of Las Vegas, soon allowed sanctioned MMA events.

The Unified Rules gave every commission one shared text to adopt. A fighter licensed in one state could expect the same fouls, rounds and weight limits in another. That shared rule book is what separates a league from a string of one-night shows. Promoters could also plan a national calendar of events around it.

words.w: Unified Rules of Mixed Martial Arts
words.d: the shared rule book first adopted by New Jersey regulators in 2001
the company that bought the UFC in January 2001
officially approved and supervised by a governing body

lessons.title: Where Commissions Came From
lessons.mainIdea: State athletic commissions were first created to regulate professional boxing, and MMA later joined the sports they license.
reading: New York passed the *Walker Law* in 1920, legalizing professional boxing under state control. It created the New York State Athletic Commission to license boxers, referees and promoters. The law was named for State Senator James J. Walker, later mayor of New York City.

Other states followed with their own commissions. Nevada created its State Athletic Commission in 1941. Las Vegas later became a center of big boxing events, which made Nevada's commission one of the most watched in the country. Walker's law replaced an earlier ban on public prize fights in the state.

A commission's main tools are licenses, medical exams, inspectors and suspensions. It can refuse to license a fighter who fails a medical test. When MMA sought approval, it entered this older system that boxing had built over eighty years. Doctors appointed by the commission examine fighters before and after bouts.

words.d: a 1920 New York law that legalized professional boxing under a state commission
a government office that licenses and regulates combat sports
an order that stops a licensed person from competing for a period of time

lessons.title: Weight Classes on Paper
lessons.mainIdea: The Unified Rules divide fighters into weight classes, so a bout sheet always names a class and a limit.
reading: Early UFC tournaments matched fighters of any size. The Unified Rules replaced that with *weight classes*, groups of fighters within set limits of body weight. Boxing had used weight classes since the late 1800s, and MMA borrowed the idea. Under the Unified Rules, each class has its own upper weight limit in pounds.

Fighters step on a scale at an official *weigh-in*, usually the day before a bout. A commission inspector records each weight on paper. A fighter who comes in over the limit can be fined or have the bout changed. Commissions set these rules to reduce dangerous weight cutting before fights.

Weight classes changed who could compete. Smaller athletes, including many wrestlers and judo players from lighter divisions, could build careers. The classes also made each division a separate ranking, much like boxing's championship belts. Women's divisions were added later with their own limits.

words.d: a group of fighters within a set range of body weight
the official weighing of fighters before a bout
one weight class and its own rankings and champion

lessons.title: The Last State to Say Yes
lessons.mainIdea: State by state, commissions licensed MMA, and New York became the last state to legalize professional MMA in 2016.
reading: In 2009 the *Association of Boxing Commissions*, a national group of state and tribal regulators, adopted the Unified Rules. Most states already licensed MMA by then. The shared rule book made the sport look the same from one state to the next. Tribal regulators oversee events held on the lands of Native American nations.

New York held out. A 1997 state law had banned professional MMA events. Lawmakers debated the ban for years, and in 2016 New York passed a law to legalize and regulate the sport. The state had allowed amateur events under rules, but professional bouts stayed banned. Supporters argued for jobs and tax money; opponents argued about safety.

UFC 205 was held at Madison Square Garden in New York City in November 2016. The event followed nearly twenty years of the ban. With New York's vote, professional MMA could be licensed in all fifty states. That event drew a large paying crowd at the Garden.

words.d: a national group of state and tribal combat sports regulators in North America
to make something allowed by law
to control an activity with official rules

sections.title: A League Built From Other Rooms

lessons.title: Borrowed Rooms
lessons.mainIdea: MMA athletes train by borrowing from older institutions: school wrestling rooms, boxing gyms, judo clubs, Brazilian jiu-jitsu academies and Muay Thai camps.
reading: Many successful MMA fighters came from American high school and college *wrestling*. That pipeline ran through bodies like the NCAA and state high school associations, which in Illinois means the IHSA. Their first training rooms were school gyms, not MMA gyms.

Other fighters came from boxing gyms, judo clubs, Brazilian jiu-jitsu academies and Muay Thai camps in Thailand. Each of those rooms kept its own ranks, rules and teachers. Many MMA athletes held ranks or records in one of them before they turned pro.

In the 2000s a new kind of *MMA gym* grew up to combine these sources in one building. Its coaches often held separate credentials from separate arts. Historians describe MMA as a league that borrows rooms, not as a single old art with one founder. Wrestling and Brazilian jiu-jitsu coaches often worked beside boxing and Muay Thai coaches there.

words.d: a grappling sport with a long school and Olympic history
a training center that combines coaches from several combat sports
a regular path that carries athletes from one institution to another

lessons.title: Women Enter the Octagon
lessons.mainIdea: The UFC held its first women's bout in February 2013, and its first women's champion came from Olympic judo.
reading: Women fought in smaller MMA promotions before the UFC admitted them. Strikeforce, a California promotion, featured women's bouts in the late 2000s. UFC leaders had said publicly that women would not fight in the company. Female fighters had built records in Japan, the United States and other countries.

That changed in February 2013 at UFC 157 in Anaheim, California. Ronda Rousey defended her bantamweight title against Liz Carmouche, a U.S. Marine veteran. It was the first women's bout in UFC history. Rousey won the bout in the first round. Carmouche was the first openly gay fighter in the UFC.

Rousey had won a bronze medal in *judo* at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, the first Olympic judo medal for an American woman. Her path ran from a judo club to the Olympics to MMA. Her career shows the league borrowing an older room and its *Olympic* record.

words.d: a Japanese grappling sport founded by Kanō Jigorō, on the Olympic program
part of the Olympic Games, run by the International Olympic Committee
a championship held by one fighter in a division

lessons.title: Television Builds the League
lessons.mainIdea: The reality series The Ultimate Fighter, first aired in 2005, brought MMA from pay-per-view to regular cable television.
reading: Zuffa lost money in its first years with the UFC. In 2005 it launched *The Ultimate Fighter*, a reality series on the cable channel Spike TV. Young fighters lived in one house, trained on teams and competed for a UFC contract. The UFC paid to produce the first season.

The first season's finale in April 2005 aired free on cable. A close bout between Forrest Griffin and Stephan Bonnar drew a large audience. Many business histories of the sport treat that night as the start of its growth. Dana White awarded contracts to both fighters after the bout.

The show made MMA a *league* with seasons, rankings and stars that viewers followed week to week. In 2016 the Fertittas and White's group sold the UFC to a group led by the talent agency WME-IMG. The deal was reported at about four billion dollars. By then the UFC held events on several continents.

words.d: a reality television series that began on Spike TV in 2005
an organized set of teams or athletes who compete under shared rules and schedules
a television show that films real people instead of actors reading a script
